prompt.context: Our client is a 350-bed hospital in a mid-size city. The organization has historically exhibited strong financial performance, and had a 1-3% operating gain each year for the last five years. However, they are projecting a $12 million operating loss this year, and expect this situation to worsen in the future. As a result, the CFO believes that they will be out of cash within five years. They are one of the largest employers in the market, and will not consider layoffs as a possible solution.
prompt.question: They have asked us to identify the source of this sudden downturn, and to come up with alternatives to restore them to a break-even position.

clarifying_info.a: Revenues have dropped approximately 15% so far this year due to aggressive pricing on capitated managed care contracts signed in January, and declining admissions and length of stay for fee-for-service contracts (mostly reimbursed on a per diem basis). All contracts are binding for three years and cannot be renegotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What is the hospital's occupancy rate and cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: Hospital occupancy is approximately 70%, resulting in high fixed costs not covered by the current contribution margin. The organization is currently staffed for 80% occupancy.

clarifying_info.q: What is the utilization of diagnostic and therapeutic services?
clarifying_info.a: Utilization of diagnostic and therapeutic services during a patient's stay is approximately 15% higher than what was expected when contract pricing was negotiated.

clarifying_info.q: What does the local competitive market look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are two other 350-bed hospitals in the city. One is an academic medical center, the other a catholic hospital recently acquired by a for-profit chain. Total admissions in the marketplace have dropped by 5% and total patient days have declined 10%.

framework: Revenue: assess changes to payer mix, contract terms (capitated vs. fee-for-service), admissions volume, length of stay
Costs (Fixed): evaluate whether fixed costs are covered given current ~70% occupancy vs. staffing for 80%
Costs (Variable): examine resource utilization per patient stay, including diagnostic and therapeutic services
Constraints: layoffs ruled out; contracts locked for 3 years, cannot be renegotiated
Solutions — Cost side: physician behavior/incentives, purchasing efficiencies
Solutions — Revenue side: new insurer contracts, affiliated physician org, Centers of Excellence
Solutions — Structural: market consolidation or affiliation with a competitor

questions.prompt: What are the key drivers of the projected $12M operating loss?
questions.guidance: Candidate should break down profit = revenue - costs. On revenue: 15% drop due to (1) aggressive capitated managed care contract pricing and (2) declining admissions and length of stay on fee-for-service contracts. On costs: high fixed costs given 70% occupancy (staffed for 80%), and variable costs elevated because resource utilization per patient stay is ~15% above the level assumed in contract pricing. Layoffs are not an option.

questions.prompt: How would you reduce costs given the constraints?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: (1) Changing physician behavior — physicians control resource utilization; align MD incentives with hospital goals by sharing risk, sharing data on their resource use vs. peers/competitors, education. (2) Purchasing efficiencies — exclusive distributor contracts for volume discounts, limit pharmacy formulary to generics, reduce vendor choice for high-volume items (prosthetics, heart catheters). Candidate should recognize that staffing cuts are ruled out but other variable cost levers exist.

Strong answers cover: (1) Sign contracts with additional insurers to grow payer base. (2) Put salaried physicians on staff to guarantee admissions to the client's hospital. (3) Create an affiliated physician organization to increase share of admissions. (4) Develop Centers of Excellence that can be marketed to managed care contractors as an exclusive regional (or supra-regional) provider for specialized services.

questions.prompt: Are there any structural or market-level solutions?
questions.guidance: Candidate should consider market consolidation: with three 350-bed hospitals and falling total market admissions (-5%) and patient days (-10%), there is excess capacity. The hospital could explore affiliating with a competitor to rationalize services across institutions, potentially allowing one hospital to close — reducing fixed costs industry-wide and improving the client's utilization and margins.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the ways the hospital could restore profitability?

categories.name: Revenue — Contracting & Volume
ideas: Put salaried physicians on staff to guarantee admissions
Create an affiliated physician organization to increase admissions share

categories.name: Revenue — Differentiation
ideas: Develop Centers of Excellence marketed to managed care contractors as exclusive regional providers
Market specialized services outside the region

categories.name: Cost — Clinical Utilization
ideas: Change physician behavior through incentive alignment and risk-sharing
Share data with physicians on their resource use vs. peers

categories.name: Cost — Purchasing
ideas: Sign exclusive distributor contracts for volume discounts
Reduce vendor count for high-volume items (prosthetics, heart catheters)

categories.name: Structural / Market
ideas: Affiliate with a competitor to rationalize market capacity
Enable service rationalization across institutions to allow one hospital to potentially close
Merge or partnership to reduce aggregate fixed costs

recommendation: The $12M loss is driven by a ~15% revenue drop (locked-in capitated contracts with aggressive pricing + lower admissions/LOS) combined with high fixed costs at 70% occupancy and variable costs running 15% above contract assumptions.

In the near term (within the 3-year contract lock-in), the hospital should focus on (1) reducing clinical resource utilization through physician incentive alignment and purchasing efficiencies, and (2) growing admissions through new insurer contracts and an affiliated physician organization.

In the medium term, the hospital should develop Centers of Excellence to differentiate and grow revenue, and explore strategic affiliation with one of the two competitors to rationalize market capacity and reduce the fixed cost burden across the city.
risks: Contracts cannot be renegotiated for three years, limiting revenue recovery speed
Physician behavior change takes time; savings may not materialize quickly
Market consolidation or affiliation is complex and may face regulatory scrutiny
Layoff restriction limits the fastest cost lever
next_steps: Quantify the cost savings achievable from physician utilization reduction and purchasing efficiencies
Model scenarios for new insurer contract revenue uplift
Assess feasibility of a Centers of Excellence strategy given existing capabilities
Explore strategic affiliation options with the two competing hospitals
